The sun at the Junction of St. Jude never sets. It lingers three degrees above the horizon, suspended in an eternal amber twilight smelling of burning birch and ozone. The station is a cathedral of cast iron and green glass, where pigeons sleep on high rafters like dusty gargoyles. Beyond the signal tower, the gray haze thickens into a dense fog that swallows iron, steam, and sound alike.

My name is Julian, though names carry little weight here. I am the collector of fares.

Every evening—or what passes for evening here—the bell atop the board tolls three times. It is a long sound, resonant as a cello string plucked in a stone cellar. The locomotives at Platform Four are vast, coal-black beasts with boilers glowing like forge fires. The passengers who step onto the platform have only one destination left, and they cannot pay with coin.

Gold is useless here. Paper money rots in the damp pockets of travel coats. The only currency accepted by the trainmen is a memory.

I sit behind a high window of polished mahogany and brass wire. Before me lies a velvet-lined tray and a small pair of silver tweezers. My task is simple: I weigh the memory offered, measure its emotional density, and issue the appropriate ticket.

Most travelers bring light, superficial things: the taste of a bitter turnip, the name of a teacher they disliked, or the sound of rain on an unfamiliar roof. These buy a ticket to third-class—the drafty wooden benches where frost creeps through floorboards and the journey feels long and cold.

To sit in the parlor cars, where armchairs are velvet and hot tea is served in blue china, requires something heavier. It costs a first love, the exact smell of a mother’s kitchen, or the sharp grief of burying a dog that lived fifteen years by your hearth.

This afternoon, a woman approached my window. She wore a coat the color of dried lavender, frayed at the cuffs, and held her hands tucked into a worn velvet muff. Her eyes were bright, clear, and utterly hollow, like windows in an abandoned cottage through which one can see only the empty sky.

"Where are you heading?" I asked her. My voice was dry from long stretches of silence.

"Somewhere quiet," she said. Her voice sounded like dry autumn leaves scraping across flagstones. "Somewhere where I don't have to remember the sound of the front door closing."

She reached up, pressed two fingers against her temple, and drew forth a shimmering thread of gold light. It hung from her fingertips like web, humming softly with a sound like beehives in summer. She laid it upon my velvet tray.

I brought down my magnifying loupe and leaned over the glass.

The memory expanded under the lens. A small dining room filled with late sun. A table laid for two, but one plate untouched. A clock ticking on the mantelpiece. A hand reaching for a brass doorknob, hesitating, then turning it. The decisive slam of wood. Then, silence—a vast, suffocating silence stretching thirty years.

"This is heavy," I told her softly. "It carries three decades of waiting. It is dense as lead."

"Can I get a carriage with a stove?" she asked. Her shoulders were hunched forward, as if shielding herself against a frost only she could feel. "My bones have been cold since late October."

"You can have the private compartment on Carriage Two," I replied. "It features a brass stove, a feather mattress, and heavy wool blankets. You will sleep uninterrupted until the end of the line."

I took the silver tweezers, lifted the glowing thread, and lowered it into a crystal flask. The moment the cork was pressed into place, the woman’s shoulders dropped. The stoop of thirty years vanished. She blinked, looked around the iron station as if noticing the vaulted arches for the first time, and smiled a calm, peaceful smile.

"Thank you," she said softly, though she no longer remembered what she was thanking me for. She took her gilded cardstock ticket and walked toward the idling train.

I sealed the flask and placed it on the towering wooden shelves behind me, beside thousands of others.

Sometimes I wonder what becomes of them all. The shelves stretch into the shadows of the roof, lost in rising steam. Some flasks glow crimson—memories of passion and betrayal. Others are pale blue, holding moments of peace: watching falling stars over a prairie, or the first time seeing the ocean.

I have my own flask, though it does not sit on the shelf. It rests in my waistcoat pocket, flat against my ribs, warm as a pocket watch.

I have been the stationmaster at St. Jude for centuries, or perhaps only since this morning. Time does not accumulate here; it merely circles like dust in the amber light. I cannot recall the name of my childhood home, nor the face of my mother. I traded all of those away long ago to secure this post.

I kept only one.

When the platform clears and the train gives its final echoing whistle, I pull the small glass vial from my pocket and hold it up to the golden sky. Inside, a tiny spark of yellow light dances.

It is a Tuesday in May. I am nine years old, sitting on the top rail of a wooden fence, eating a ripe peach. The juice runs down my wrist, sticky and sweet. My dog barks at a yellow butterfly in the clover below, and my father is whistling from the barn—a song whose name I forgot long ago. The air smells of crushed grass, river silt, and approaching summer. Nothing bad has happened yet.

The train chugs once, grinding its heavy steel wheels against the tracks as it pulls out toward the white fog. I slip the vial back into my waistcoat pocket, pick up my feather duster, and wait for the next traveler.
